key_terms.meaning: A crystal develops electric charge when mechanically stressed; stress → charge.
An applied voltage changes the crystal's shape; used to transmit ultrasound.
Op-amp circuit that converts tiny piezoelectric charge into a low-impedance voltage.
Time a sound pulse out and back; distance d = v t / 2, with v the speed of sound in the medium (343 m/s in air, about 1540 m/s in tissue).
Z = ρ c; a mismatch at a boundary reflects sound.
Proof mass on a spring-damper whose relative motion indicates vibration.
Seismic transducer used below resonance, with output proportional to acceleration.
V<sub>H</sub> = R<sub>H</sub> I B / t for a strip of thickness t.
R<sub>H</sub> = 1/(n q) for one carrier type; its sign shows carrier type.
A magnetic material changes length when magnetized.
Stress changes the magnetization or permeability of a magnetic material.
Device that turns light into an electrical signal.
Light guided in a fibre; strain or temperature changes intensity, phase or wavelength.
Produces a pulse count; position comes from counting, and a datum is needed.
Gives a unique code for each position, so no count is lost after a power cut.
Small generator whose voltage is proportional to shaft speed.
Flashing light at adjustable frequency that freezes a rotating mark for speed measurement.
Feedback coil force cancels the input force; coil current measures force or pressure.
Electrode in a photomultiplier tube that emits secondary electrons and multiplies current.
Measures light absorbed by a sample versus wavelength to find concentration.
Δf = 2 f v cos α / c; blood or particle speed from the frequency shift of the echo.
Absolute-encoder code in which neighbouring positions differ in one bit; resolution 360°/2ⁿ for n tracks.
G = δⁿ for n dynodes of secondary emission ratio δ; anode current I<sub>a</sub> = G I<sub>k</sub>.
A = −log₁₀ T = ε c l; absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length.

takeaways: Piezoelectric sensors suit dynamic force, pressure, vibration and ultrasound; a charge amplifier conditions their tiny charge.
Ultrasonic sensors use echo time or Doppler shift for distance, level and flow without touching the target.
A seismic mass on a spring and damper reads acceleration below resonance and displacement above resonance.
Hall effect sensors measure magnetic field, current or position without contact.
Magnetostrictive and magneto-elastic sensors link stress and magnetization, so they sense force, torque and position and make sound waves.
Photoelectric and fibre optic sensors convert light changes into electrical signals and allow remote or distributed measurement.
Incremental encoders count pulses, while absolute encoders give a unique code for every position.
Speed can come from a tachogenerator voltage, a stroboscope flash or a signal frequency; force-balance feedback gives high accuracy.
Photoemissive tubes (phototube, PMT) give the highest sensitivity; a scintillator in front of a PMT counts gamma rays and measures their energy, as in a gamma camera.

Photodiodes, phototransistors, photovoltaic and photoconductive cells trade speed, linearity and cost; a photodiode with a transimpedance amplifier is the usual spectrophotometer and pulse-oximeter detector.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for construction, working principle, formula, signal conditioning, a comparison and one practical application, not just definitions. Biomedical syllabi stress the photoelectric devices (phototube, photomultiplier, scintillation counter, photodiodes, phototransistors, photovoltaic and photoconductive cells, their comparison and spectrophotometric uses) and the piezoelectric transducer as a pressure and ultrasound transducer.

bank.q: Explain the piezoelectric effect and the inverse piezoelectric effect. Describe a charge amplifier circuit used to condition the output of a piezoelectric pressure transducer.
outline: Crystal equivalent circuit as charge source with capacitance
Output voltage proportional to charge, not cable capacitance
Applications: dynamic pressure, vibration, ultrasound transmitter and receiver
answer: Direct effect. Certain crystals without a centre of symmetry (quartz, Rochelle salt) and poled ceramics (PZT) or polymers (PVDF) develop charge on their faces when stressed. The charge is proportional to force: Q = d F, with d the charge coefficient in C/N (quartz 2.3 pC/N, PZT 300 to 600 pC/N). Removing the force brings the charge back to zero; reversing the force (tension instead of compression) reverses its sign.

Inverse effect. A voltage across the same crystal produces a strain proportional to the field. The crystal can therefore transmit as well as sense, which is why one PZT element sends and receives ultrasound.

Pressure transducer construction. A thin steel diaphragm, welded to the housing, faces the process. Behind it a stack of n quartz plates under preload collects the diaphragm force F = P A. Thin foil electrodes between the plates are wired in parallel, so the charges add: q = n d A P. A low-noise coaxial cable takes the charge to the amplifier.

Equivalent circuit. The crystal is a charge source q in parallel with its capacitance Cc = ε0 εr A / t and leakage resistance R. A voltage amplifier would read V = q / (Cc + Ck + Cin), so its gain depends on the cable capacitance Ck, and the charge leaks away with τ = R C, so the sensor cannot hold a static pressure.

answer.text: Charge amplifier. The crystal feeds the inverting input of an op-amp with a feedback capacitor Cf and a large resistor Rf across it; the non-inverting input is grounded. The inverting input is a virtual ground, so no voltage builds up across Cc or Ck and all of q flows onto Cf:
answer.pre:
V<sub>out</sub> = − q / C<sub>f</sub>
f<sub>L</sub> = 1 / (2π R<sub>f</sub> C<sub>f</sub>)   (lower cut-off; R<sub>f</sub> stops the output drifting)

answer.text: Worked numbers. Engine cylinder pressure: two quartz plates (n = 2, d = 2.3 pC/N, each 1 cm² and 1 mm thick), P = 2 MPa, Cf = 1 nF, Rf = 10 GΩ.

head: Quantity
Working
Value
rows: Voltage amplifier, 2 m cable (200 pF) + 10 pF input
Voltage amplifier, 5 m cable (500 pF) + 10 pF input

answer: Reading the numbers. Changing the cable from 2 m to 5 m more than halves the voltage-amplifier reading, but the charge amplifier stays at −0.92 V. Its 0.016 Hz cut-off is far below the 25 Hz firing rate of a four-stroke engine at 3000 rpm (one firing every two turns: 3000 / 60 / 2 = 25 Hz), so the pressure waveform passes undistorted.

Signal chain and applications. Charge amplifier, low-pass filter, then a recorder or ADC. Uses: engine and blast pressure, vibration and shock, ultrasound transmitters and receivers, and in medicine pulse and heart-sound pickups and ultrasound probes.
Check. Vout × Cf = 0.92 V × 1 nF = 0.92 nC = 920 pC, the charge computed from n d A P.

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of a photomultiplier tube and explain how it is used with a scintillation counter.
outline: Photocathode emits electrons by photoelectric effect
Dynode chain gives secondary emission multiplication
Gain depends on number of dynodes and voltage
PMT converts light to a current pulse
Use in low-light and radiation counting
answer: Construction. An evacuated glass tube holds a window and a photocathode (for example bialkali or caesium antimonide), a focusing electrode, a chain of dynodes (typically 8 to 12) coated with a secondary-emission material, and an anode. A resistor divider across a high-voltage supply (about 1 to 2 kV) holds each dynode 80 to 150 V above the one before.

Photoemission. A photon with energy above the work function frees a photoelectron from the cathode. The quantum efficiency η (often 0.2 to 0.3) is the number of photoelectrons per photon. The cathode current is Ik = η e Φp.

Multiplication. The focusing field sends the photoelectron into dynode 1; it strikes with about 100 eV and knocks out δ secondary electrons. These are pulled to dynode 2, and so on. After n dynodes the gain is G = δⁿ and Ia = G Ik. With δ = 4 and n = 10: G = 4¹⁰ = 1 048 576 ≈ 1.05 × 10⁶. Because δ rises with the dynode voltage, the supply must be stable: a small change in voltage changes the gain far more.

Timing and noise. The transit time (cathode to anode) is tens of nanoseconds; its spread sets the timing resolution. Thermionic emission from the cathode gives dark pulses, which the gain multiplies; cooling and a pulse-height discriminator reduce them.

Scintillation counter. A NaI(Tl) crystal, sealed against moisture, is optically coupled to the PMT window. A gamma ray that stops in the crystal produces a flash whose number of photons is proportional to the energy deposited (about 38 photons per keV for NaI(Tl)). The PMT turns each flash into one current pulse.

Block diagram. High-voltage supply → crystal + PMT → preamplifier → linear amplifier → pulse-height analyser (discriminator or multichannel analyser) → counter or spectrum display. The preamplifier sits next to the tube so the small charge pulse does not travel down a long cable.

answer.text: Worked numbers. A 140 keV gamma ray of technetium-99m, fully absorbed; take all the light reaching the cathode, η = 0.25 and the PMT above.
answer.pre:
photons        = 140 keV × 38 per keV = 5320
photoelectrons = 0.25 × 5320 = 1330
anode charge   = 1330 × 1.05×10⁶ × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C = 2.23×10⁻¹⁰ C
pulse on 100 pF = 2.23×10⁻¹⁰ / 100×10⁻¹² = 2.23 V

answer: Use. The pulse height (2.23 V here) is proportional to the gamma energy, so the analyser can accept 140 keV pulses and reject scattered, lower-energy ones; the count rate gives activity. This is how survey meters, well counters and the gamma camera of nuclear medicine work.
Check. Doubling the energy to 280 keV doubles the photons to 10 640 and the pulse to 4.46 V, as a linear energy scale requires.

bank.q: Compare phototube, photomultiplier tube, photodiode, phototransistor, photovoltaic cell and photoconductive cell.
outline: Output type: current, voltage or resistance
answer: Principles. Phototube and PMT: photoemission into vacuum (the PMT adds dynode gain). Photodiode: photocurrent from electron-hole pairs in a reverse-biased or zero-biased junction. Phototransistor: the photodiode current is the base current, multiplied by β. Photovoltaic cell: an unbiased junction that generates voltage and power. Photoconductive cell (LDR): a semiconductor film whose resistance falls with light.

head: Device
Output
Sensitivity
Speed
Linearity, dark current
Typical use
Limitation
rows: about 1 kV, magnetic fields upset it, costly
medium (≈ 0.5 A/W at 850 nm in Si)
small signal needs a transimpedance amplifier

answer.text: Same light on each device. Take 1.0 nW of 420 nm light (2.11 × 10⁹ photons per second, from the PMT example of the chapter).

answer: Reading the table. At 1 nW only the PMT gives a signal far above the nanoampere dark currents of the semiconductor devices, which is why PMTs serve photon counting and dim ultraviolet work. At microwatt levels the photodiode is enough and is preferred for its linearity, size and low voltage.

Choosing. Precise, linear measurement (spectrophotometry, pulse oximetry): photodiode. Very low light or radiation counting: PMT. On/off sensing at low cost: phototransistor or LDR. Power: photovoltaic cell.
Check. PMT to photodiode output ratio: 84.5 µA / 0.2 nA = 4.2 × 10⁵, roughly the PMT gain (10⁶) times the ratio of their cathode-to-diode efficiencies (84.5 pA / 200 pA = 0.42).

bank.q: Explain the Hall effect. Derive the Hall voltage for a thin rectangular semiconductor strip and list practical applications.
outline: Charge separation creates transverse electric field
Equilibrium gives V<sub>H</sub> = R<sub>H</sub> I B / t
Sign of Hall voltage gives carrier type
Applications: magnetic field measurement, current sensing, proximity and position
answer: Set-up. A thin plate of n-type semiconductor, width w, thickness t, carries a current I along its length. A field B is applied perpendicular to its face. The electrons drift with velocity v opposite to I.
Force on the carriers. Each electron feels the Lorentz force F = e v B sideways, so electrons gather on one edge and leave positive charge on the other. The charge sets up a transverse field EH.

answer.text: Derivation. In equilibrium the electric force balances the magnetic force:
answer.pre:
e E<sub>H</sub> = e v B   →   E<sub>H</sub> = v B
I = n e v w t   →   v = I / (n e w t)
V<sub>H</sub> = E<sub>H</sub> w = I B / (n e t)
V<sub>H</sub> = R<sub>H</sub> I B / t,   with R<sub>H</sub> = 1 / (n e)

answer: Meaning. VH rises with I and B and falls with thickness and carrier density, so thin, lightly doped, high-mobility plates (InSb, GaAs) are used. In p-type material the carriers are holes, RH is positive and VH has the opposite sign, so the sign of VH tells the carrier type.

answer.text: Numbers for the InSb plate of the chapter (RH = 3.8 × 10⁻⁴ m³/C, t = 0.1 mm, w = 2 mm, I = 10 mA, B = 0.2 T):

answer: Practical sensor. Constant-current drive, a differential amplifier on the same chip, offset trimming (the side contacts are never exactly opposite) and temperature compensation. A Schmitt trigger gives a switch output.

Applications. Flux-density meters (gaussmeters); clamp-on current sensors (a 2 mm ring gap around 50 A gives B = μ0 I / g = 31.4 mT, read as 1.19 mV by the plate above); proximity and position switches; gear-tooth speed sensing; brushless motor commutation, including in pumps and ventilators; phone compasses.
Check. The formula directly: VH = RH I B / t = 3.8×10⁻⁴ × 0.01 × 0.2 / 10⁻⁴ = 7.6 mV, the same as EH w.

bank.q: Explain a seismic transducer with a mass, spring and damper. Distinguish between an accelerometer and a vibrometer.
outline: Below resonance: output proportional to acceleration
Above resonance: output proportional to displacement
answer: Construction. A case fixed to the vibrating body holds a seismic mass m on a spring k with a damper c. A sensing element (piezoelectric crystal, strain gauge, LVDT or capacitor) measures the relative displacement z = x − y between mass and case.

answer.text: Equation of motion. With case motion y and mass motion x:
answer.pre:
m z¨ + c z˙ + k z = − m y¨
ω<sub>n</sub> = √(k/m),   ζ = c / (2√(k m)),   r = ω / ω<sub>n</sub>
for y = Y sin ωt:
  Z / Y        = r² / √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)      (displacement response)
  Z ω<sub>n</sub>² / A  = 1 / √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)      (acceleration response)

answer: Accelerometer (r ≪ 1). The denominator is close to 1, so Z ≈ A/ωn²: the output is proportional to acceleration. Needs a high natural frequency: small mass, stiff spring.

Vibrometer or seismometer (r ≫ 1). Z/Y → 1: the mass stays almost still in space and the case moves around it, so the output is the displacement. Needs a low natural frequency: large mass, soft spring.
Damping. ζ ≈ 0.7 removes the resonance peak, widens the flat band (within 1 % up to r ≈ 0.4 for an accelerometer) and gives a nearly linear phase, so waveforms keep their shape.

Reading the numbers. The vibrometer spring would sag 0.248 m under its own mass, which is why low-frequency seismometers use pendulum or force-feedback designs instead of a simple hanging mass; the accelerometer moves only nanometres.

Applications. Accelerometers: machine condition monitoring, airbags, phones, body-worn activity and tremor monitors, rate-responsive pacemakers. Vibrometers and seismometers: ground motion, building vibration.
Check. For the accelerometer, ωn² = k/m = 4×10⁸ s⁻², so 1 g gives Z = 9.81 / 4×10⁸ = 24.5 nm, consistent with a stiff, high-fn design.

bank.q: Design an ultrasonic level sensor for a water tank. Explain echo timing, temperature compensation and beam selection.
outline: Transmit pulse and measure echo delay
Level from time and speed of sound
answer: Arrangement. A 40 kHz piezoelectric transducer at the top of a 3.0 m tank faces down at the water surface. It sends a burst, then listens; the echo time t gives the air gap d = v t / 2, and the level is h = H − d.
Temperature compensation. The speed of sound in air rises about 0.6 m/s per °C: v ≈ 331.3 + 0.606 T (T in °C). A temperature sensor in the head recomputes v for every reading.

answer.text: Worked reading. Air at 30 °C, echo at 10.0 ms.

answer: Beam selection. With a 25 mm transducer, λ = 349.5 / 40 000 = 8.74 mm and sin θ = 1.22 λ / D = 1.22 × 8.74 / 25 = 0.426, so θ = 25.2°. At 1.75 m the spot radius is 1.75 × tan 25.2° = 0.82 m, so the sensor must be mounted well away from walls, ladders and inlet pipes, which would give false echoes. A larger face or a higher frequency narrows the cone.
Blind zone. The transducer rings for about 1 ms after the burst, so echoes from closer than 349.5 × 0.001 / 2 = 0.17 m are lost. The maximum level must stay at least this far below the face.

Echo detection. A time-varying gain raises amplification for later echoes; a threshold or the first peak above a noise floor stops the timer; averaging several pings rejects splashes, and a gate ignores echoes outside the expected window.
Output. For a 4 to 20 mA transmitter over 0 to 3 m: I = 4 + 16 × 1.253 / 3 = 10.68 mA.
Check. 10.68 mA reads back as (10.68 − 4)/16 × 3 = 1.253 m, and t = 2 × 1.747 / 349.5 = 10.0 ms, the measured echo time.

bank.q: A press needs dynamic force measurement. Compare a piezoelectric sensor with a strain-gauge load cell and recommend one with signal conditioning.
outline: Piezoelectric: charge output, dynamic, high stiffness
Strain gauge: resistive bridge, good static response
answer: Requirement. A press applies 20 kN pulses at about 10 strokes per second. The sensor must follow fast force changes, be very stiff so it does not change the press dynamics, and survive overload.

Piezoelectric load washer. A quartz ring under the tool gives q = d F. Its stiffness is very high (natural frequency in the tens of kilohertz), deflection is a few micrometres, and range and overload capacity are large. It cannot hold a static force: the charge leaks with τ = Rf Cf.

Strain-gauge load cell. Four gauges on an elastic element in a full bridge give a voltage proportional to strain. It measures static force accurately, but the elastic element must strain about 1000 µε, so it is softer and its natural frequency is lower.

head: Sensor
Working
Result
rows: Strain-gauge bridge, 10 V, GF 2, ±1000 µε, four active arms

answer: Signal conditioning. Piezo: charge amplifier with a reset or range switch and a low-pass filter; output several volts, so no further gain is needed. Load cell: regulated excitation, instrumentation amplifier (gain about 250 to bring 20 mV to 5 V), low-pass filter and shunt calibration.

Mounting and temperature. Both need flat, parallel seats and a central preload for the washer. Quartz has a small temperature coefficient but pyroelectric ceramics do not; the load-cell bridge self-compensates for temperature if all four gauges are matched.

Recommendation. For the dynamic 10 Hz force, choose the piezoelectric washer with a charge amplifier: fL = 0.016 Hz is far below 10 Hz, it is stiffer and gives volts of output. Add a strain-gauge cell only if the press must also hold and measure a static force.
Check. A 10 Hz pulse lasting about 50 ms loses 1 − e−0.05/10 = 0.5 % of its charge during the pulse, small enough for process monitoring.

bank.q: Use an incremental encoder with quadrature output to measure the position and direction of a machine table. Explain resolution, datum and pulse counting.
outline: A and B channels in quadrature
Resolution from pulses per revolution and lead screw pitch
answer: Set-up. A rotary incremental encoder of N = 500 slots is coupled to the lead screw of a machine table with pitch p = 5 mm. Each turn of the screw moves the table 5 mm.
Quadrature. Two tracks A and B are a quarter of a slot pitch apart, so their square waves are 90° apart. Counting every edge of both gives 4 counts per slot.

answer.pre:
counts per turn = 4 N = 4 × 500 = 2000
resolution      = 5 mm / 2000 = 2.5 µm per count
table move 120 mm → 120 / 0.0025 = 48 000 counts

answer: Direction. If B rises before A (state sequence 00 → 01 → 11 → 10), the decoder adds 1 at each edge; if A leads, the same states come in reverse and it subtracts 1. Direction is read live from the phase order.

Counter circuit. A and B pass through line receivers and Schmitt triggers, are sampled on a fast clock, and a state machine compares each AB pair with the last one to give up or down pulses to a 32-bit counter. Position = count × 2.5 µm.
Datum. At start-up the table runs slowly to a home switch, then to the next Z (index) pulse, and the counter is loaded with zero. All later positions are measured from this datum.

Speed limit. At a table speed of 50 mm/s the screw turns 10 rev/s; channel A runs at 10 × 500 = 5 kHz and the counter must accept 4 × 5 kHz = 20 kHz count edges, well within a microcontroller encoder interface.

Resolution is not accuracy. The 2.5 µm count is the smallest step the controller can see, but the table position also depends on the lead-screw pitch error, backlash in the nut and twist of the screw. A ball screw with a preloaded nut and a pitch-error table in the controller brings the accuracy close to the resolution; for the best machines a linear scale on the table itself replaces the rotary encoder.

Power-failure limitation. When power is lost the count is lost, and a table pushed by hand while off is not tracked, so homing must be repeated (or an absolute encoder or battery-backed counter used).
Check. 48 000 counts × 2.5 µm = 120 000 µm = 120 mm, the table movement.

bank.q: Set up a fibre optic strain sensor. Explain intensity or phase modulation, source, fibre and detector choices.
outline: Strain changes fibre length or refractive index
Intensity modulation or interferometric phase modulation
Advantages: EMI immunity and remote sensing
answer: Source. A stable LED or superluminescent diode for intensity sensors; a narrow laser for interferometric sensors; a broadband source for fibre Bragg gratings (FBG).

Fibre. Multimode fibre suits intensity sensing (high NA collects more light); single-mode fibre is needed for phase and FBG sensing. The fibre is bonded along the strained structure or embedded in it.

Intensity modulation. Strain bends the fibre between corrugated plates (microbending) and light leaks out, so the received power falls with strain. Simple and cheap, but a change in source power or connector loss looks like strain, so a reference fibre or ratiometric reading is needed.

Phase modulation. Strain changes the fibre length and refractive index, shifting the phase of light in a sensing arm against a reference arm (Mach-Zehnder interferometer). Very sensitive, but temperature also shifts the phase and the fringes must be counted.

answer.text: Wavelength modulation (FBG). A grating in the core reflects one wavelength λB; strain shifts it. At 1550 nm the shift is about 0.78 λB per unit strain:

answer: Temperature compensation. An FBG also shifts about 10 pm per °C, so a 5 °C change (50 pm) would read as about 41 µε. A second grating, loose (strain-free) beside the first, measures temperature alone and its shift is subtracted.
Detector. A photodiode with a transimpedance amplifier for intensity; a pair of photodiodes in the interferometer; a spectrometer or tunable-filter interrogator for FBGs.

Intensity-sensor numbers. A microbend sensor passes 50 µW at zero strain and loses 0.5 µW per 100 µε. A 0.5 A/W photodiode gives 25 µA and −0.25 µA per 100 µε; a 100 kΩ transimpedance amplifier gives 2.5 V and −25 mV per 100 µε. A 2 % drift of the LED moves the output by 0.02 × 2.5 V = 50 mV, which would read as 50 / 25 × 100 = 200 µε. That is why a reference channel is essential.
Advantages. Immune to electrical noise, no current at the sensing point (safe in explosive areas and inside MRI scanners), light, long-distance, and many FBGs can share one fibre.
Check. 0.60 nm / 1.21 pm per µε = 496 µε ≈ 500 µε, the applied strain.

bank.q: Measure the speed of a motor using a tachogenerator and using a stroboscope. Compare the two methods.
outline: Stroboscope freezes a mark at flash frequency
Speed from flash frequency and mark count
answer: Tachogenerator. A small permanent-magnet DC generator coupled to the shaft gives E = K ω. A filter removes commutator ripple and a high-resistance voltmeter, scaled in rpm, reads it.
Reading. With K = 0.05 V/(rad/s) at 1500 rpm: ω = 1500 × 2π / 60 = 157.08 rad/s, E = 7.85 V; ripple at 12 segments × 1500 / 60 = 300 Hz.
Loading. With armature resistance Ra = 50 Ω and a 10 kΩ meter, V = 7.85 × 10 000 / 10 050 = 7.81 V, which the scale reads as 1492 rpm, 0.5 % low. A higher-resistance meter removes most of this error.

Ripple filter. A first-order RC low-pass with its corner at 30 Hz, a tenth of the ripple frequency, needs R = 10 kΩ and C = 1/(2π × 10 000 × 30) = 0.53 µF; at 300 Hz it passes 1/√(1 + 10²) = 0.0995 of the ripple, about a tenth. An AC tachogenerator avoids the commutator but needs a rectifier, or its frequency f = p n / 60 can be counted instead.

Stroboscope. A xenon flash at an adjustable rate f lights a single painted mark. When f equals the speed in revolutions per second the mark appears frozen. Start at a high rate and lower it: the first single still mark is the true speed. At 1500 flashes per minute one still mark appears; at 3000 two marks 180° apart appear, confirming 1500 rpm.

Calibration. The tachogenerator needs K, found against a reference speed; the stroboscope depends only on its flash-rate oscillator, which is easy to make accurate, so it often calibrates the tachogenerator.

head: Feature
Tachogenerator
Stroboscope
rows: down to low speed, both directions (DC)
needs a periodic motion, fails at very low speed

answer: Check. 7.85 V / 0.05 = 157 rad/s × 60 / 2π = 1500 rpm, and the strobe at 1500 flashes/min gives the same.

bank.q: Analyse the errors in an ultrasonic distance measurement caused by temperature and air movement. Compare this method with a Hall proximity sensor for position measurement.
outline: Speed of sound changes with temperature
Air currents and reflections cause error
Hall sensor needs a magnetic target and measures field change
answer: Temperature. d = v t / 2 assumes a value of v. The speed in air is about v = 331.3 + 0.606 T: 343.4 m/s at 20 °C and 355.5 m/s at 40 °C, 3.5 % higher.

answer.text: Error example. A target 2.000 m away on a 40 °C day, with the sensor still using the 20 °C speed:

answer: Air movement. A wind w along the path: t = d/(v + w) + d/(v − w). For w = 5 m/s and d = 2 m, t = 11.66 ms and the reading is 343 × t / 2 = 2.0004 m, only 0.02 % long, because the gain one way almost cancels the loss the other way. Crosswinds and temperature layers bend the beam, and turbulence makes the echo jitter, which matters more than the axial error.

Other errors. Blind zone near the face, soft or angled targets that send the echo away, foam and dust absorbing sound, side lobes hitting nearby objects, and the threshold triggering at different points on a weak and a strong echo.

Hall proximity sensor. A magnet on the moving part changes the field at a Hall sensor. Field falls quickly with distance; for a small magnet, roughly as 1/x³ far from it: 100 mT at 2 mm becomes 12.5 mT at 4 mm and 0.8 mT at 10 mm. So the useful range is a few millimetres to a few centimetres, but in that range the sensor is fast, rugged and unaffected by temperature of the air, dust or sound.

head: Feature
Ultrasonic
Hall proximity
rows: needs a magnet (or ferrous target with a bias magnet)
works in oil, dirt; stray fields can disturb

answer: Choice. Liquid level or the distance to a person or vehicle: ultrasonic with temperature compensation. Cylinder end position, door closed, gear-tooth speed: Hall sensor.
Check. Correcting the 40 °C reading with the right speed: 355.5 × 0.01125 / 2 = 2.000 m.

bank.q: Evaluate piezoelectric, magnetostrictive and force-balance methods for force measurement under static and dynamic conditions.
outline: Magnetostrictive: stress changes magnetization, good for torque and force
Force-balance: feedback null, high accuracy, static and dynamic
answer: Static and dynamic needs. A static force (a weight, a clamping force) must be held for minutes without drift; a dynamic force (impacts, vibration) needs bandwidth and stiffness. The three methods suit these differently.

Piezoelectric. Charge q = d F into a charge amplifier. Very stiff, wide bandwidth (to tens of kilohertz), large range. But the charge leaks with τ = Rf Cf: with Cf = 10 nF and Rf = 10 GΩ, τ = 100 s, and a static 20 kN read after 10 s has decayed to e−10/100 = 0.905 of its value, 9.5 % low. So it is a dynamic method; quasi-static use needs a reset just before the event and a short measurement.

Magnetostrictive. Stress changes the permeability of a magnetic core (Villari effect); in a load cell two windings at right angles see a coupling that grows with force. It measures static and dynamic force, is extremely rugged (rolling mills, crane hooks) and takes overloads, but has hysteresis and nonlinearity, needs a stable bias, and its accuracy is about 0.5 to 1 %, not better.

Force balance. A coil drives the beam back to null, and I = F/(B L) measures force. With B = 0.25 T and L = 50 m, 2 N needs 0.16 A (0.08 A/N). It holds static forces with no drift from springs and is the most accurate (laboratory balances work this way), but the range is set by the coil current: a 0.5 A limit gives Fmax = 0.5 × 12.5 = 6.25 N, and the loop settles in tens of milliseconds, so bandwidth is low.
Recommendation. Impact or vibration force: piezoelectric. Heavy industrial static loads in a harsh place: magnetostrictive. Small precise static forces and weighing: force balance.
Check. The force-balance scale: 6.25 N × 0.08 A/N = 0.5 A, the coil limit; the piezo decay: 20 kN × 0.905 = 18.1 kN read after 10 s.

bank.q: Evaluate the choice of photoelectric transducer for spectrophotometric concentration measurement, including dark current, noise, linearity and wavelength range.
answer: Measurement. The instrument compares the light through a blank (I0) with the light through the sample (I): T = I/I0, A = −log₁₀ T = ε c l. The detector must be linear over the range of I, have low dark current, and respond at the wavelength used.
Path. Lamp (tungsten for visible, deuterium for ultraviolet) → monochromator → cuvette → detector → amplifier → readout of A or c.

Photodiode. Linear over many decades, small, low voltage, about 0.5 A/W in the red, lower in the blue and ultraviolet unless UV-enhanced; read with a transimpedance amplifier. Best for routine visible work and clinical analysers.

Photomultiplier tube. Gain near 10⁶ gives the best sensitivity for weak light (narrow slits, ultraviolet, high absorbance), and the bialkali cathode covers roughly the ultraviolet and visible. It needs a stable kilovolt supply and its dark counts must be subtracted.

answer.text: Dark current and stray light at high absorbance. Blank photocurrent 20 µA, sample at A = 2 (1 % transmitted, 0.20 µA).

answer: Linearity and saturation. Stray light and detector nonlinearity bend the calibration line above A ≈ 2, so samples are diluted or a shorter cell used. A PMT can saturate at high light, so its gain is lowered for the blank.

Wavelength range. A silicon photodiode covers about 190 to 1100 nm with UV enhancement; a bialkali PMT is strongest in the blue and near ultraviolet; for near-infrared work InGaAs photodiodes are used.

Readout numbers. With 0.45 A/W and the 44.4 µW blank, the photodiode gives 20 µA and a 100 kΩ transimpedance amplifier 2.00 V. At A = 2 the sample gives only 20 mV. A 16-bit converter on a 2.5 V range has steps of 2.5 / 65 536 = 38 µV, so the absorbance step at A = 2 is 0.434 × 38 µV / 20 mV = 0.0008: adequate, but offsets of a few hundred microvolts in the amplifier would matter, so the dark reading is taken with the shutter closed and subtracted.
Choice. A photodiode for most clinical and teaching spectrophotometers (haemoglobin at 540 nm, glucose and cholesterol colour reactions); a PMT for low-light ultraviolet work or fluorescence.
Check. With dark current subtracted and no stray light, −log₁₀(0.20/20) = 2.000, the true absorbance.

bank.q: Compare incremental and absolute encoders for a CNC axis. Discuss power failure, resolution, cost and interface.
outline: Choice for CNC safety and start-up
answer: Incremental encoder. Gives A, B and Z pulses; position is a count from a datum. Cheap, few wires, very fine resolution, but the count is lost at power-off, so the axis must be homed.
Absolute encoder. Gives a unique code (Gray code read as binary) for every position; multi-turn types also count turns with gears or a battery-free counter. Position is known at power-on.

answer.text: Resolution on a ball-screw axis of pitch 10 mm.

answer: Interface. Incremental: differential A, A̅, B, B̅, Z, Z̅ lines (RS-422) to a counter; at 3000 rpm a 2048-line encoder runs at 2048 × 3000 / 60 = 102.4 kHz per channel and 409.6 kHz counts, which the counter must accept. Absolute: a serial link (SSI, BiSS, EnDat) sends the position word with a check code, using fewer wires than parallel outputs.

Noise immunity. A noise spike on an incremental line adds or loses a count permanently until the next homing. An absolute word is read fresh each time, so a bad read is a single wrong sample that the check code can reject.
Cost. Incremental encoders are cheaper; absolute multi-turn encoders cost more but save the homing hardware and time.

Safety and start-up. After a power cut or emergency stop, an absolute axis knows where it is and can retract the tool safely; an incremental axis must home first, which may be impossible with a tool in the work.
Choice for a CNC axis. An absolute multi-turn encoder for safety and fast start-up on production machines; an incremental encoder where cost matters and homing at each start is acceptable.
Check. Both encoders give 8192 steps per turn, so both resolve 10 mm / 8192 = 1.22 µm; the difference is in what happens at power-on, not in resolution.
